The Lighthouse Keeper

For forty-one winters, Mara Halloran kept the light on Corrow Point burning,
and in all that time nobody ever asked her to.

The Board had sent a letter once, in her second year, confirming her wages and
the schedule of oil deliveries. After that there was only the sea. She learned
the moods of it the way other people learn a language: the flat grey patience
of August, the black hammering of February, the strange green calm that came
before the worst of it.

She trimmed the wick at dusk. She wound the clockwork that turned the lens.
She wrote the weather in a ledger nobody read, in handwriting that got smaller
every decade, as though she were trying to make the years fit.

In the winter she turned seventy-three, the light went out.

Not the lamp — the lamp was fine. The island went dark: the generator, the
radio, the small electric bulb over her kitchen table. She sat in the sudden
black and listened to the storm find its shape, and understood that the ships
out there could not see her.

So she climbed. Two hundred and eleven steps with a can of oil and a box of
matches, in the dark, at seventy-three. She lit the old lamp by hand, the way
the first keeper had in 1868, and she stayed beside it turning the lens with
her own arms because the clockwork needed power she did not have.

She turned it all night. Her shoulders gave out somewhere near four in the
morning and she kept turning anyway, counting rotations aloud to stay awake,
and when the grey came up over the water she was still there, still turning,
with her hands stiff around the handle.

The trawler *Bright Endeavour* made harbour at seven. Eleven men aboard. Their
captain said afterwards that he had steered by a light that swung strangely,
slower than it should, but never once stopped.

Nobody had asked her to do that either.

They gave her a medal the following spring, in a hall in the town, and she was
polite about it. But she told the girl who came to interview her that the medal
had it wrong. It was not brave, she said. Bravery is a thing you decide.

She had simply never considered letting it go out.
